Executive Summary

RELEASE PREVENTION AND EMERGENCY RESPONSE POLICIES

The Lallemand Bio-Ingredients USA LLC (Lallemand) facility in Hutchinson, Minnesota has a good record in preventing releases of anhydrous ammonia (ammonia). As part of their release prevention program, the plant has a detailed preventive maintenance program.
The facility has implemented an Emergency Action Plan to ensure the safety of its employees, the community, and the environment. The emergency response program includes procedures for handling an emergency and notes that external responding  team (Hutchinson Fire Department) is HAZMAT-trained. The emergency response policies at the Lallemand facility ensure that there is emergency response coverage 24 hours per day and 7 days per week.

PROCESS DESCRIPTION AND REGULATED SUBSTANCES

Lallemand produces food grade yeast. The NAICS code for the process at this facility is 311999.  The facility uses and stores the following EPA-regulated substance(s) in quantities exceeding threshold limits under 40 CFR Part 68:
-	Anhydrous Ammonia (CAS No. 7664-41-7). Stored in pressurized vessel exceeding the 10,000 lb threshold. 
Substance(s) is/are used in-process and not as fuel or refrigerant, and thus do not qualify for exemptions under §68.126 or other exclusions.

OFFSITE CONSEQUENCE ANALYSIS (OCA)

Worst-Case Scenario
The largest potential release of ammonia would occur with a puncture in the ammonia tank. Taking the specific definition of the worst-case from 40 CFR 68.25, the largest quantity of ammonia that can be stored in a vessel is in the ammonia tank during a pump out condition. The total quantity of ammonia that can be stored in a single ammonia tank is over 55,000 pounds. Since the facility is located in a semi-populated area, the toxic cloud formed by the evaporating ammonia would reach offsite endpoints and nearby receptors.

Alternative Release Scenario
The alternative release scenario that meets the selection criteria is an ammonia release f

rom a pipe flange. The release is located outside, approximately 8 feet above ground level. Administrative controls are not applicable to this scenario. Active mitigation of the release is through human intervention. Since the facility is located in a semi-populated area, the toxic cloud formed by the evaporating ammonia would reach offsite endpoints and nearby receptors.
Modeling was performed using EPAs RMP*Comp and/or ALOHA with conservative meteorological assumptions as required.

GENERAL ACCIDENTAL RELEASE PREVENTION PROGRAM AND CHEMICAL-SPECIFIC PREVENTION STEPS

The facility follows Program 3 prevention elements for ammonia and ethanol, including, among others:

- Process hazard analysis (PHA)
- Operating procedures and training
- Mechanical integrity and preventive maintenance
- Management of change (MOC)
- Incident investigation and compliance audits

Design, controls, and procedures are intended to meet the requirements of OSHA PSM (29 CFR 1910.119) and EPA RMP standards.
Listed below are some key aspects of the release prevention program:
1. Most of the equipment at the ground level is guarded against impact.
2. Critical ammonia equipment is installed above the 100 year flood level.
3. Most of the pipe work is out of the way of people and machinery thus there is less chance of a release due to incidental equipment damage.

FIVE-YEAR ACCIDENT HISTORY

In the five years preceding this submittal, the facility has had no accidental releases of regulated substance(s) that resulted in offsite impacts including injuries, evacuations, or environmental damage.

EMERGENCY RESPONSE PROGRAM

The facility maintains an up-to-date Emergency Response Plan under 40 CFR §68.95 and coordinates with the local fire department, emergency medical services, and the county LEPC. Key elements include:

- Procedures for notification, evacuation, and mitigation
- Coordination with emergency responders
- Periodic drills and plan updates
- Communication with potentially affected neig

hbors

PLANNED CHANGES TO IMPROVE SAFETY

The facility is committed to continuously improving safety and minimizing the potential for accidental releases of regulated substances. Ongoing and planned improvements include:
	Implementing recommendations resulting from Process Hazard Analyses (PHAs) and compliance audits
	Enhancing contractor safety, employee training, and employee participation programs
	Engaging a third-party consultant with PSM and RMP expertise to assist with targeted improvements across multiple program elements, including:
o	Delivering initial and refresher PSM/RMP training for management personnel
o	Strengthening the RMP management system
o	Integrating facility-specific best practices into the PSM/RMP compliance framework
o	Reviewing and updating the contractor safety program
o	Revamping the employee training program and implementing a comprehensive tracking matrix
o	Supporting the timely closure of corrective actions
